subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the Edexcel spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE Edexcel Sociology simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: 'Primary data' is data that is...
options: Collected first-hand by the researcher themselves
questions.explain: Primary data is gathered first-hand by the researcher, e.g. through their own survey or interviews.

questions.q: A sociologist using government census statistics collected by someone else is using...
questions.explain: The census is produced by others, so using it is secondary data.

questions.q: 'Quantitative data' is best described as...
options: Data in the form of words and meanings
Numerical data that can be counted or measured
questions.explain: Quantitative data is numerical/statistical and can be counted and compared.

questions.q: In-depth quotes about how people feel about their jobs are an example of...
questions.explain: Rich, descriptive information about feelings and meanings is qualitative data.

questions.q: A 'sampling frame' is...
options: The final results of a study
A list of all members of the target population from which a sample is drawn
questions.explain: A sampling frame is the list of the population from which a sample is selected.

questions.q: In 'random sampling', participants are chosen so that...
options: Every member of the population has an equal chance of selection
Only the first 10 people are used
questions.explain: Random sampling gives everyone in the sampling frame an equal chance of being chosen.

questions.q: A researcher who asks each participant to recommend others, building the sample gradually, is using...
questions.explain: Snowball sampling grows through referrals, useful for hard-to-reach groups.

questions.q: A strength of questionnaires is that they...
options: Can be distributed to large numbers of people quickly and cheaply
questions.explain: Questionnaires are cheap, quick and can reach many respondents, producing comparable data.

questions.q: A limitation of postal questionnaires is that they often have...
questions.explain: Postal questionnaires typically suffer from low response rates, which can bias results.

questions.q: A 'structured interview' uses...
options: The same set of pre-set, standardised questions for every respondent
questions.explain: Structured interviews use identical, standardised questions, making them reliable and comparable.

questions.q: Unstructured interviews are praised by interpretivists mainly because they produce...
options: Rich, valid qualitative data about meanings
questions.explain: Unstructured interviews are flexible and generate deep, valid qualitative insight into meanings.

questions.q: In 'covert' participant observation, the researcher...
options: Tells the group they are being studied
Joins the group without revealing they are a researcher
questions.explain: Covert observation hides the researcher's identity, which raises ethical problems around consent.

questions.q: A strength of participant observation is that it can produce...
options: Valid, in-depth data by seeing behaviour in its natural setting
questions.explain: Participant observation gives rich, valid data by studying people in their natural context.

questions.q: In a laboratory experiment, the researcher controls variables in order to...
options: Establish cause and effect under controlled conditions
questions.explain: Lab experiments control variables to test cause and effect, though they can lack ecological validity.

questions.q: Personal documents such as diaries and letters are examples of...
questions.explain: Diaries and letters are secondary, qualitative sources offering insight into people's lives.

questions.q: Research is 'reliable' when...
options: It can be repeated and produces consistent results
It measures what it claims to measure
questions.explain: Reliability means a study can be replicated with consistent results.

questions.q: Research has high 'validity' when the data...
options: Gives a true, accurate picture of what is being studied
questions.explain: Validity is about accuracy: whether the data genuinely reflects reality.

questions.q: Which of the following is a key ethical requirement in sociological research?
options: Gaining informed consent and protecting participants from harm
questions.explain: Ethical research requires informed consent, confidentiality and protection from harm.

questions.q: Guaranteeing that participants' identities are kept private is called...
questions.explain: Keeping participants' identities private is confidentiality/anonymity, a core ethical duty.

questions.q: A 'hypothesis' is...
options: The final conclusion of a study
A testable prediction or statement to be investigated
questions.explain: A hypothesis is a testable statement or prediction that the research sets out to investigate.
